articles.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
articles.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.
articles.content:
Scientists have reconstructed a remarkably detailed family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo, tracing their origins back to the moment a fertilized egg first divided into two cells. Using an innovative DNA recording technology, the researchers followed how those early cells multiplied, developed specialized roles, and eventually helped form a body with distinct organs and tissues.

The recording covered the first 13.5 days of embryonic development, providing an unusually detailed look at how a complex mammalian body takes shape. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.)

The findings, published on October 8, 2026, in the journal Science, could help scientists better understand normal development and what happens when that process goes wrong.

"We are interested in tracking how cells' early ancestry in an embryo influences their later fates. Exploring cell lineages helps decode normal development. Such research could eventually advance knowledge about congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental conditions, genetic disorders or cancer," said Dr. Jay Shendure, a professor of genome sciences at the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator.

Shendure led the research alongside Dr. Chengxiang Qiu, a molecular and systems biologist at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Both served as senior authors of the study.

A DNA Typewriter Records the History of Living Cells

The achievement was made possible by a technology called DNA Typewriter, developed by Shendure and Junhong Choi, who is now at Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.

Rather than simply observing cells as they divide, the system allows scientists to preserve a record of their history directly within their DNA.

To accomplish this, the researchers inserted a redesigned recording sequence, which they call a tape, into the genome of a fertilized mouse egg. The updated design made it easier to recover the information stored in individual cells.

As the embryo developed, the DNA Typewriter remained embedded in the genetic material of its cells, recording their divisions in a way that could later be used to reconstruct their ancestry. The result was something like a biological logbook, documenting the sequence of events that gave rise to different cell populations.

"Think of it like an actual typewriter, except it types onto a cell's own DNA instead of paper," explained Haedong Kim, a co-first author of the study and a postdoctoral scientist in genome sciences at UW Medicine, the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. "Every time a cell divides, it strikes one new character onto the next blank line -- always in order, never overwriting what's already there. Because the characters are always filled in sequence, that sequence itself spells out the cell's division history."

Because these markings are passed down to daughter cells, researchers can examine the recorded sequences and identify which cells descended from a shared ancestor. Cells carrying matching portions of the record can be linked together, allowing scientists to reconstruct branches of the embryo's family tree.

"Writing the record is only half the problem. You also have to read it back out of each cell, so we redesigned the tape to make that easier," said Kim.

Overcoming a Major Challenge in Developmental Biology

Reconstructing the entire history of a developing mammal has long been a formidable challenge. As an embryo grows, its cells divide repeatedly and begin taking on specialized functions. Following those relationships becomes increasingly difficult as the number and variety of cells expand.

Scientists accomplished a similar feat decades ago in a tiny roundworm, but that animal has a relatively simple body with far fewer cells. Its transparency also makes development easier to study.

Mammals are considerably more complicated. Earlier technologies provided important insights into mouse embryonic development, but they generally captured only portions of the larger cellular family tree.

Some traditional recording techniques also have significant limitations. They work by cutting DNA to create identifying marks, which can damage cells and erase information left by earlier divisions. Their recording capacity is limited, and because the marks are not necessarily created in a fixed sequence, scientists must attempt to reconstruct the order of events afterward.

"DNA Typewriter avoids all of this," said Kim. "It writes without fully severing the DNA, keeps recording relatively steadily, and writes everything in strict order, so we can record cell lineages at much higher resolution for a longer time."

Tracing an Embryo Back to Its First Two Cells

The researchers began by attempting to record development in 100 fertilized mouse eggs. Of those, 10 embryos were ultimately available for examination.

One specimen, identified as Embryo No. 3, stood out because its DNA recording system had functioned particularly well and preserved the most extensive developmental history. The scientists therefore concentrated their detailed analysis on that embryo.

One of the most important discoveries came from a recording made at the very beginning of development, immediately after the fertilized egg divided for the first time.

"Our recording captured a clear, permanent mark distinguishing the two very first cells, letting us trace nearly every cell we profiled from the embryo back to one or the other," said Kim. "One of these two founding cells did go on to produce more descendants than the other, but they produced diverse cell types at almost equal ratios."

This meant that although one of the original cells contributed more descendants overall, both founding cells gave rise to a remarkably similar mix of specialized cell types.

The finding illustrates how scientists can now investigate the earliest stages of development with a level of detail that was previously difficult to achieve.

Scientists Discover When Cells Choose Their Roles

The DNA recordings also revealed important information about when cells begin committing to their eventual roles in the body.

Early embryonic cells can give rise to many different types of tissue. As development progresses, their descendants gradually become more specialized, eventually forming structures such as the nervous system, skin, blood, and eyes.

By reconstructing the branches of the embryo's cellular family tree, the researchers could determine when different groups of cells began following distinct developmental paths.

Their observations were consistent with conclusions drawn from decades of previous research, but the new approach allowed them to examine these patterns within a single developing mouse.

"Blood cells and the retina committed relatively early, while the skin's outer layer didn't commit until noticeably later," the researchers explained. "Cell fate wasn't locked in all at once. Different cell types settled into their identity on their own separate schedules, some early and some late."

These findings show that the transition from a flexible, unspecialized cell to one with a particular biological function does not happen at the same time throughout the embryo.

Instead, different tissues follow their own developmental timelines. Some cells begin narrowing their possible futures early, while others remain flexible for a longer period before becoming committed to a specific role.

What This Could Mean for Birth Defects, Cancer, and Stem Cell Therapies

Understanding exactly how cells acquire their identities could eventually have important implications for medicine.

Many developmental disorders arise when the normal process of cell specialization or tissue formation is disrupted. Cancer also involves abnormal cell behavior, including failures in the mechanisms that ordinarily regulate cell growth and division.

By tracing cellular ancestry and identifying when different developmental pathways emerge, scientists may gain a clearer understanding of how these problems begin.

"This kind of large-scale developmental recording gives scientists a map of how one cell becomes a whole body -- which helps explain how organs form correctly, how that process can go wrong in birth defects, and how abnormal cell growth drives cancer. As stem cell engineering advances, this kind of recording can also help guide how we engineer cells for therapeutic use."

Although the work was conducted in mouse embryos and does not yet represent a direct medical treatment, it demonstrates a powerful way to study the biological decisions that shape a developing organism.

The approach could also support future stem cell research, particularly efforts to guide cells toward specific identities for regenerative medicine and other therapeutic applications.

Research Team and Funding

Additional co-first authors included Qi Yu and Sophie Seidel, both affiliated with the University of Washington School of Medicine's Department of Genome Sciences and the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology.

Shendure serves as the lead scientific director of the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology. He is also scientific director of the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine and the Allen Institute for Cell Lineage Tracing.

The research received support from the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology, a collaboration involving the Allen Institute, BioHub, and University of Washington School of Medicine (CZIF2023-008738); the Paul G. Allen Frontiers Group's Allen Discovery Center for Cell Lineage Tracing; the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine; the Washington Research Foundation; the National Institutes of Health (R00HG012973 and P30CA008748); the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation (DFS-64-24); the Searle Scholars Award (SSP-2025-101); Dartmouth's Center for Quantitative Biology through a National Institute of General Medical Sciences grant (P20GM130454); and the Swiss National Science Foundation (239394).

This advance has broad implications for understanding birth defects, genetic disorders, cancer, and stem cell therapies, representing a meaningful positive impact on health research with potential large-scale benefits.

This tool writes a record of each cell division directly into the cell’s DNA, like typing on a biological notebook. They tracked development from the first two cells up to 13.5 days, revealing how cells multiplied and became specialized.

**Impact** – This study shows when different cells decide what role they will play in the body, such as blood or skin cells, and that these decisions happen at different times. articles.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
articles.summary: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.
articles.content:
Feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong? Everyday habits such as eating a nutritious breakfast, getting regular exercise, and sleeping enough may play an important role in how well your mind handles difficult situations.

New research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.

Psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change. Rather than becoming trapped in negative thinking or overwhelmed by frustration, people with greater psychological flexibility can recognize their emotions, consider their options, and respond in a more productive way.

"You might know someone who stays cool under pressure," said Lina Begdache, an associate professor of health and wellness studies at Binghamton University and lead author of the research. "The kind of person who misses a flight and, instead of panicking, calmly adapts to the situation. This person may still feel stressed, but they're better able to manage it through psychological flexibility."

"People may say that these are resilient people, but they also have what's called psychological flexibility. They're able to change the way they think about the situation and then use brain resources to handle the stress."

How Breakfast, Sleep, and Exercise Relate to Mental Resilience

To explore the relationship between lifestyle choices and emotional resilience, Begdache worked with Jason Cherry, a former Binghamton assistant professor of physical therapy, and former student Alexander J. Talkachov.

The researchers collected anonymous survey responses from approximately 400 college students, gathering information about their diets, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle factors.

Their findings revealed an important connection between healthy routines and the ability to cope with stress. Students who reported healthier habits, including regular physical activity and consistent breakfast consumption, also tended to demonstrate greater psychological flexibility and resilience.

The study identified several notable associations:

Regular breakfast consumption: Eating breakfast at least five times per week was associated with greater resilience, with psychological flexibility helping explain the relationship.

Eating breakfast at least five times per week was associated with greater resilience, with psychological flexibility helping explain the relationship. Adequate sleep: Students who slept fewer than six hours generally reported lower levels of both resilience and psychological flexibility.

Students who slept fewer than six hours generally reported lower levels of both resilience and psychological flexibility. Physical activity: Exercise lasting 20 minutes or longer was associated with greater psychological flexibility and an improved ability to cope with stress.

Exercise lasting 20 minutes or longer was associated with greater psychological flexibility and an improved ability to cope with stress. Fish oil intake: Taking fish oil several times per week was linked to better psychological flexibility.

The opposite pattern also emerged. Students who reported less healthy behaviors, including frequent fast food consumption and insufficient sleep, tended to show greater psychological rigidity, meaning they had more difficulty adjusting their thoughts and behaviors when circumstances changed.

Because the research relied on survey responses, the results demonstrate associations rather than proving that these habits directly improve psychological flexibility or resilience.

Why Psychological Flexibility Matters for Stress

According to Begdache, psychological flexibility gives people the mental space to recognize what they are experiencing instead of becoming completely absorbed by their stress. This ability to reassess a situation can make it easier to understand difficult emotions and determine how to respond.

She explained that improvements in diet and lifestyle may help support this kind of mental adaptability.

"When we're under stress, we feel like we fuse with the stress. We live the stress. But psychological flexibility is like stepping back and thinking, 'I feel this because of that. What can I do?' Identifying your emotions sometimes helps you find the solution for these emotions," said Begdache.

The findings also build on Begdache's previous research, which linked nutritious diets to greater resilience and poorer dietary habits to reduced resilience.

The latest study offers a possible explanation for that relationship. Rather than influencing resilience alone, diet and lifestyle may support psychological flexibility, which in turn helps people manage stress more effectively.

"The new finding here is that diet and lifestyle don't just make you resilient by themselves. They help you build the psychological flexibility, which, in turn, makes you a resilient person."

The study, "Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator," was published in the Journal of American College Health.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a scientific study demonstrating that common healthy lifestyle habits like eating breakfast, exercising, and sleeping well are linked to greater psychological flexibility, which helps people better manage stress. This has broad significance for mental health and wellbeing, offering actionable insights for the general public. The study is well-contextualized and focused on a single topic with clear positive implications for improving resilience and mental adaptability.

articles.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.
articles.content:
Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.

Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.

"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease."

Researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.

Their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.

The findings were published in Nature.

Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain

To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.

The team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.

The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.

Many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.

"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," says D'Angelo.

Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps

The new atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.

One striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.

"This shows that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal important features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.

Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids

Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered new insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.

When researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.

The cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, showed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an important component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.

These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.

"Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," says Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs."

A New Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.

By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.

The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.

"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in brain research with the creation of a detailed 3D lipid map revealing 539 distinct chemical zones. This discovery fills a major knowledge gap about brain chemistry, has broad implications for understanding brain function, aging, and diseases like Alzheimer's and depression, and provides a valuable tool for the global scientific community. The impact is meaningful for public health and neuroscience, and the article provides substantial context and detail about the methodology and findings.

The findings also show how lipids act like chemical "postal codes," linking distant brain parts with similar roles. This map is a valuable tool for scientists studying brain health, aging, and diseases like Alzheimer’s.

**What's next step** – The Lipid Brain Atlas is available online for scientists worldwide. Researchers can use it with other brain data to better understand brain function and how lipid changes affect diseases. Although this map is for mice, the method can help create similar maps for humans in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have made the first detailed 3D map of brain lipids, revealing 539 unique chemical regions that improve understanding of brain organization and changes during pregnancy.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising paradox in how our cells age
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that the body's cellular recycling system behaves very differently during aging than previously believed, with higher activity sometimes linked to worse physical health. A small study suggests that even gentle exercise could help restore more youthful cellular recycling patterns in older adults.
articles.content:
Cells rely on a natural cleanup system to prevent damaged materials from accumulating inside them. Known as autophagy, this process collects defective proteins and other cellular waste, packages them into specialized compartments, and breaks them down into basic molecular components that can be reused.

This recycling system helps protect cells from damage. Scientists have long considered declining autophagy a hallmark of aging, and problems with the process have been linked to numerous diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders.

However, new research suggests that cellular recycling does not necessarily slow down as people get older. Instead, its activity can increase, decrease, or remain unchanged depending on the type of cell and a person's sex. The findings also suggest that exercise may influence how this process functions in older adults.

Researchers at Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute reported these findings on September 27, 2026, in the journal Aging Cell, challenging a widely accepted view of how cellular recycling changes throughout life.

"We commonly see people cite this idea that autophagy declines with age, but the actual evidence for this in humans is very thin," said senior and corresponding author Caroline Kumsta, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Interest is growing in targeting autophagy to develop new healthy aging interventions," said Tatiana Moreno, PhD '26, lead author of the study and a former graduate student in the Kumsta lab.

"We wanted to challenge assumptions and investigate what actually happens to autophagy during aging in healthy individuals."

How Scientists Studied Cellular Recycling and Aging

To better understand the relationship between aging and autophagy, the researchers collected blood and skin samples from volunteers between the ages of 23 and 72. All participants reported having no chronic medical conditions.

The team also converted some of the collected skin cells into induced neurons, allowing the researchers to examine cellular recycling in three different cell types.

For each cell type, the scientists analyzed RNA transcripts, which are produced when cells read genetic instructions from DNA to make proteins, enzymes, and other essential components. This analysis allowed them to examine how age and cell type affected the activity of genes involved in autophagy.

Importantly, the researchers did not rely on gene activity alone. They also directly measured how quickly cells carried out autophagy, allowing them to determine whether patterns in gene expression accurately reflected the amount of recycling taking place.

The results revealed a much more complicated picture than the traditional understanding of cellular aging.

"We found that autophagic activity changes were not universal throughout the body and did not follow the idea that autophagy simply declines with age," said Kumsta. "Rather, cellular recycling rates are altered differently with age in each of the cell types, and differently by sex in each of the cell types."

Aging Affects Different Cells in Surprising Ways

The researchers observed striking differences in how autophagy changed with age. In skin cells from male participants, recycling activity decreased as age increased. In female skin cells, it remained relatively stable. Meanwhile, induced neurons derived from female participants showed an increase in autophagy with age.

These findings demonstrate that cellular recycling does not follow a single pattern throughout the body. Instead, aging appears to affect the process differently depending on the cells being examined and the sex of the individual.

The researchers also discovered that the expression of genes responsible for autophagy did not reliably indicate how much recycling was actually occurring. Cells with higher or lower levels of autophagy gene expression did not necessarily show corresponding differences in their measured recycling rates.

"This shows that people using static measures such as transcription levels to infer what's happening with autophagy need to be really careful about their interpretations," said Moreno.

Why More Cellular Cleanup May Not Be Better

The team next investigated whether differences in autophagy were associated with physical health and performance as people age.

Their findings pointed to another unexpected possibility: higher levels of cellular recycling may have different implications for younger and older adults.

Among participants aged 70 and older, greater autophagy activity was associated with poorer measures of physical function across all three cell types studied.

In blood cells, higher autophagy was linked to lower aerobic fitness. In skin cells, it was associated with a higher body mass index (BMI). In induced neurons, increased recycling activity was connected to weaker grip strength, lower metabolism, and a higher resting heart rate.

These associations suggest that increased autophagy is not necessarily a sign of healthier aging. Although cellular recycling plays an essential protective role, its relationship with physical health may change later in life.

"I think this is an important distinction that merits continued study, as it appears that increased autophagy flux may be good in younger people yet problematic in older people," said Kumsta.

"Autophagy and aging are so much more nuanced than previously assumed," said Moreno. "To better translate autophagy research discoveries into potential therapies, we really need to understand what is happening on a cell-specific level and how it is affected by sex and age."

Gentle Exercise May Help Restore Youthful Cellular Activity

The researchers also explored whether physical activity could influence autophagy in older adults.

In a small pilot study, five participants between the ages of 77 and 88 completed a gentle exercise program lasting 12 weeks. The activities focused on reducing the risk of falls, and researchers collected blood samples both before and after the program to measure changes in cellular recycling.

The preliminary results suggested that exercise could lower autophagy activity in blood cells toward levels more typical of younger adults. Participants also showed improvements in physical performance.

Although the pilot involved only five people, the findings raise the possibility that exercise could help regulate cellular recycling in ways that support healthier aging. Larger studies will be needed to establish whether these changes are consistent and how they relate to improvements in physical health.

"It is exciting to have this exercise intervention that may have a positive effect on autophagy and healthy aging, and I'm really excited to see where that goes," said Kumsta.

Expanding Research Into Exercise and Healthy Aging

The findings highlight the importance of understanding cellular recycling as a process that changes in complex ways throughout life, rather than one that uniformly declines with age. They also suggest that future treatments targeting autophagy may need to account for a person's age, sex, and the specific cells involved.

To investigate the potential benefits of exercise further, the Kumsta laboratory received a pilot grant from the Altman Clinical and Translational Research Institute at the University of California San Diego (UC San Diego).

The team is now working with the Exercise and Physical Activity Resource Center at UC San Diego on larger studies involving more participants and improved testing methods. These efforts will examine how physical activity affects autophagy, aging, and physical function, with the goal of better understanding whether changes in cellular recycling could eventually contribute to strategies for healthier aging.

Funding: The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute, National Institute on Aging, American Foundation for Aging Research, Conrad Prebys Foundation, The Howard and Maryam Newman Family Foundation, and Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust.

articles.personality_title: New study reveals surprising changes in cell recycling during aging
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Our cells have a natural system called autophagy, which cleans up damaged parts inside them to keep the body healthy. Scientists believed this cleaning process slows down as we get older, leading to health problems.

**What happened** – Researchers studied blood and skin cells from healthy people aged 23 to 72. They found that the activity of autophagy changes in different ways depending on the type of cell and whether the person is male or female. For example, in some cells from older women, autophagy actually increased. They also found that higher autophagy was linked to poorer physical health in people over 70. A small group of older adults who did gentle exercise showed signs that exercise might help restore younger patterns of autophagy.

**Impact** – This discovery changes what we thought about aging cells. Instead of autophagy just slowing down with age, it behaves differently in various cells and between men and women. It also shows that more cell cleaning isn’t always better for older adults. The link between autophagy and health is more complex than before, which is important for developing future treatments.

**What's next step** – Scientists plan to study more people and test how exercise affects autophagy and physical health in older adults. This could help create better ways to support healthy aging by targeting cell recycling processes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Cell recycling changes in surprising ways with age, and gentle exercise might help older adults maintain healthier cellular cleanup.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio revela cambios sorprendentes en el reciclaje celular durante el envejecimiento
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Nuestras células tienen un sistema natural llamado autofagia, que limpia las partes dañadas dentro de ellas para mantener el cuerpo sano. Los científicos creían que este proceso se ralentizaba con la edad, causando problemas de salud.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores estudiaron células de sangre y piel de personas sanas entre 23 y 72 años. Encontraron que la actividad de la autofagia cambia según el tipo de célula y el sexo. Por ejemplo, en algunas células de mujeres mayores, la autofagia aumentó. También vieron que más autofagia estaba relacionada con peor salud física en personas mayores de 70 años. Un pequeño grupo de adultos mayores que hicieron ejercicio suave mostró que el ejercicio podría ayudar a restaurar patrones más jóvenes de autofagia.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia lo que pensábamos sobre las células que envejecen. La autofagia no solo disminuye con la edad, sino que varía según las células y el sexo. Además, más limpieza celular no siempre es mejor para los adultos mayores. Esta complejidad es importante para crear futuros tratamientos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos planean estudiar a más personas y probar cómo el ejercicio afecta la autofagia y la salud física en adultos mayores. Esto podría ayudar a apoyar un envejecimiento más saludable.

**Resumen en una frase** – El reciclaje celular cambia de formas sorprendentes con la edad, y el ejercicio suave podría ayudar a los adultos mayores a mantener una limpieza celular más saludable.
